title: One async failure boundary
summary: Catch rejected promises, map failures to stable codes, and keep stack traces out of responses.

scenario.briefing: The status service now has several async handlers. One rejected promise escaped the request and the client received an internal stack trace. Centralize the failure path.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Review an artifact and identify the concrete risks.

hints: Attach .catch to the promise returned by the handler.

misconceptions.description: Calling an async handler without handling its promise.
misconceptions.testDescription: The wrapper catches the handler promise instead of dropping it.
misconceptions.feedback: Attach a catch or await inside a wrapper. Otherwise a rejection bypasses the response entirely.

misconceptions.description: Returning error.stack or a driver message to the client.
misconceptions.testDescription: The boundary answers with a code and never a stack trace.
misconceptions.feedback: Stack traces reveal internal paths and implementation details. Return a stable code and log the detail on the server.

misconceptions.description: Trusting an uncaughtException listener as a request boundary.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Approving the uncaughtException listener as a safe request boundary.
misconceptions.feedback: The process is already in an undefined state after an uncaught exception. Handle the handler promise per request instead.

sections.title: A promise is not a callback
sections.body: An async handler returns a promise. If nobody attaches a rejection handler, the failure becomes an unhandled rejection and the client waits for a response that never comes.

sections.title: Responses carry codes, logs carry details
sections.body: A stable error code and status tell the client what happened. Stack traces, file paths, and driver messages belong in server logs, not in the response body.

sections.title: One boundary beats many try blocks
sections.body: A wrapper gives every handler the same failure behavior. Handlers can throw a typed failure and trust the boundary to serialize it consistently.

artifact.title: status-server.ts
artifact.caption: The async handler drops its promise and the failure helper returns internal details.

findings.label: The async request handler has no catch, so a rejected promise is unhandled.
sendFailure returns the internal stack trace to the client.
Every failure is reported as 500 instead of a specific status.
The uncaughtException listener makes the process safe to keep serving.

verdicts.label: Block the change until the failure boundary is fixed.
Ship it; the failure handling is acceptable.

steps.explanation: createServer ignores the promise returned by the async handler, so a parse failure becomes an unhandled rejection. sendFailure also writes error.stack to the client, and every failure is flattened to 500. Keeping a process alive after uncaughtException is not a request boundary.
hints: Look for dropped promises and client-visible internals.
createServer does not await an async handler.
A stack trace in the body leaks implementation details.
uncaughtException is not a per-request boundary.
